fixture_notice: All scenarios, business inputs and test logs are invented teaching examples.

versions.title: Help AI find the current note
versions.article:
If AI gives you an old answer when the current note is already saved, check the route it followed. Start with one question whose answer you know, rather than reorganising the whole knowledge base. That gives you a clear way to judge whether it found the right evidence.

In this fictional example, the main router points to projects/example/index.md. The project index points to policy-current.md and policy-archived.md. The current document was updated on 10 October and requires review before sending a draft. The archived document was updated on 1 September and is marked obsolete. Your question asks for the current review requirement, so policy-current.md must supply the answer.

Ask AI to show the route from the main router, through the project index, to the current document. Then ask it to state the requirement and cite that file. You should be able to see both where the answer came from and why that source applies. A citation to the archived file would still be the wrong answer.

The index helps direct the search, but it does not prove the answer is correct. Check that its links work and that the selected document is current. This question does not require loading the entire knowledge base, although the example proves neither a token saving nor guaranteed accuracy.

Your next action is to ask AI for its route and source, then check the document's status. Keep the question small enough that you can recognise the correct result yourself.
versions.script: If AI misses a note you've saved, ask where it looked. In this fictional example, the main router points to projects/example/index.md. That index lists policy-current.md, updated 10 October, and policy-archived.md, updated 1 September and marked obsolete. The current rule requires review before sending a draft. Ask AI to follow the router, open the index, select policy-current.md and cite it in the answer. Then check the links and the document's status. An index points towards evidence; it does not prove accuracy. This question needs neither the entire knowledge base nor a promise of token savings. Your next action: ask for the route and source, then check that it selected the current policy.

versions.title: A map to the right shelf
versions.article:
Imagine asking a librarian for today's borrowing rules and being handed an old notice. The notice exists, and someone can show you where it came from, but it cannot answer a question about the current rules. Finding something and finding the right thing are different tasks.

Our fictional knowledge base has a similar arrangement. Its main router is the entrance map, pointing to projects/example/index.md. That project index acts like a shelf label: it points to policy-current.md and policy-archived.md. The current note was updated on 10 October and requires review before sending a draft. The archived note was updated on 1 September and is marked obsolete.

Picture the route as four connected stops: main router, project index, current document, answer with its source. Each stop helps the AI reach the next. When the question asks for the current review requirement, the route should end at policy-current.md. Ending at the archived note would produce the wrong answer even if the file were cited accurately.

The library analogy has a limit. A map cannot judge the truth or freshness of the book it points towards. Likewise, the index is a pointer rather than proof. Its links must work, and the selected document's status must be checked. This question does not need the entire knowledge base, but that alone establishes neither token savings nor guaranteed accuracy.

Ask AI to show its route and source, then check the document's status. The useful result is a visible path to the current evidence, rather than a bigger pile of notes.
versions.script: Imagine a library map pointing you to an obsolete notice. Finding it would not make its rules current. In our fictional example, the main router leads to projects/example/index.md, which lists two notes. Policy-current.md was updated 10 October and requires review before sending a draft. Policy-archived.md was updated 1 September and is obsolete. Follow four stops: router, project index, current document, answer with its source. The index is a map, not proof: check its links and the selected note's status. This question does not need the whole knowledge base, but no token saving or accuracy guarantee is established. Ask AI to show that route and source, then check it chose the current policy.

versions.title: A source link can still lead to the wrong answer
versions.article:
A cited answer can still be wrong if its source is obsolete. Before judging a knowledge system by how neatly it is organised, check whether it can answer a question using the document that actually applies. The important distinction is between locating a file and locating current evidence.

Consider a fictional test. The main router points to projects/example/index.md, and that project index points to two documents. Policy-current.md was updated on 10 October and requires review before sending a draft. Policy-archived.md was updated on 1 September and is marked obsolete. For a question about the current review requirement, policy-current.md is the correct source.

There are two possible outcomes to compare. If AI selects the current file, states its requirement and cites it, the answer matches the supplied evidence. If it selects the archived file, the source citation may be accurate while the answer remains unsuitable. An index alone cannot distinguish those outcomes for us.

Check the route from router to index to document, confirm that the links work, and inspect the selected document's status. Loading the whole knowledge base is unnecessary for this question. However, this invented example does not measure token savings or show that the approach guarantees accuracy on other tasks. Those would require separate evidence.

The next action is to ask AI to show its route and source, then check the document's status. Judge this particular answer against the current note before drawing a broader conclusion about the system's reliability or efficiency.
versions.script: A citation does not prove an answer is current. In this fictional test, the router leads to projects/example/index.md. That index lists policy-current.md, updated 10 October, and policy-archived.md, updated 1 September and obsolete. The current requirement is review before sending a draft. Selecting and citing policy-current.md answers the question; citing the archived file does not. Check the route, the links and the selected document's status. The whole knowledge base is unnecessary here, but this example establishes neither token savings nor guaranteed accuracy elsewhere. Your next action is to ask AI for its route and source, then check it used the current policy. Judge the answer against that evidence.

versions.title: Draft the quote, then check what is missing
versions.article:
AI can help organise an enquiry into a quote draft, but you still need to check what the customer has asked for and what remains unknown. Begin with the supplied information, show the calculation clearly, and leave gaps visible rather than filling them with guesses.

Here is a fictional decorating example. All quantities and prices are invented teaching inputs, not market rates. The enquiry specifies 20 square metres of walls. The supplied labour rate is £12 per square metre, so labour comes to £240. Add the supplied £45 materials cost and the illustrative subtotal is £285.

Write those inputs and calculations into the draft so a person can check them. Keep the scope equally clear: ceiling, doors and additional preparation are not included in the stated work. Do not treat a request to paint the walls as permission to add other surfaces or assume that every preparation task is covered.

Next, list the unanswered questions. Tax treatment, access, final surface condition and start date are unknown. The AI should leave them unresolved, rather than silently include tax or invent a date. The £285 subtotal is a calculation from the example inputs; it is not an approved final price.

Your next action is to confirm the scope and unknowns with the appropriate person, then obtain approval before sending the quote. A useful draft makes that review easier because the numbers, exclusions and unanswered questions are visible together. Completing the arithmetic does not complete the decision to send it.
versions.script: Turn an enquiry into a draft by using the supplied facts and keeping gaps visible. This decorating example is fictional; its prices are not market rates. There are 20 square metres of walls at £12 per square metre: £240 labour. Add £45 materials and the illustrative subtotal is £285. Ceiling, doors and additional preparation are outside the stated scope. Tax treatment, access, final surface condition and start date are unknown. Do not silently add tax, invent dates or call the subtotal an approved final quote. AI can show the calculation and list questions. Your next action is to confirm the scope and unknowns, then obtain a person's approval before sending.

versions.title: Follow the enquiry into a quote draft
versions.article:
Picture an enquiry moving across a desk in three stages: supplied information, a calculation, and a draft waiting for review. Information should only move into the calculation when it has actually been supplied. Unanswered questions stay visible beside the draft, rather than disappearing into a confident final price.

Our decorating example is fictional, and its quantities and prices are teaching inputs rather than market rates. The first stage contains 20 square metres of walls, a labour rate of £12 per square metre and £45 for materials. In the calculation stage, 20 multiplied by £12 produces £240 labour. Adding £45 gives an illustrative subtotal of £285.

Now picture the scope as a labelled outline around the work. It contains the specified walls. Ceiling, doors and additional preparation are outside that stated outline. The drawing would describe the supplied scope; it would not establish what the customer ultimately needs or what a decorator will approve.

Four unanswered labels remain beside the draft: tax treatment, access, final surface condition and start date. The AI can display them, but it must not turn a blank label into an invented fact. It should neither silently include tax nor choose a start date. The subtotal remains illustrative, not an approved final quote.

The last stage therefore needs a person. Your next action is to confirm the scope and unknowns, then obtain approval before sending. The diagram helps you follow how the draft was formed; the review determines whether it is ready to leave the desk.
versions.script: Picture three stages: enquiry, calculation, draft awaiting review. This decorating example is fictional, with invented inputs rather than market rates. The enquiry supplies 20 square metres of walls at £12 per square metre and £45 materials. The calculation gives £240 labour and a £285 illustrative subtotal. Draw the scope around the walls: ceiling, doors and additional preparation remain outside it. Beside the draft, keep four unknowns visible: tax treatment, access, final surface condition and start date. Those blanks must not become invented dates, silent tax assumptions or an approved final price. Your next action is to confirm the scope and unknowns, then obtain a person's approval before sending.

versions.title: Correct arithmetic is not an approved quote
versions.article:
A quote draft can contain correct arithmetic and still be unready to send. The calculation answers one question: what follows from the supplied inputs? It does not settle whether the scope is complete, whether the assumptions are acceptable or whether a person has approved the price.

Consider a fictional decorating enquiry. Its quantities and prices are invented teaching inputs, not market rates. It specifies 20 square metres of walls at a supplied labour rate of £12 per square metre. Labour is therefore £240. With the supplied £45 materials cost, the illustrative subtotal is £285. That result is supported by the example's numbers.

The limits of the calculation matter equally. Ceiling, doors and additional preparation are not in the stated scope. Tax treatment, access, final surface condition and start date are unknown. A completed-looking document would not resolve any of those questions. If AI silently included tax or invented a date, it would introduce an unsupported assumption.

We can therefore judge the draft on two separate grounds. Its arithmetic should match the supplied inputs, and its wording should preserve the exclusions and unknowns. Passing the arithmetic check does not make £285 an approved final quote. The AI may draft the calculation and list what needs clarification, but a person must confirm the scope and approve the quote before it is sent.

Your next action is to confirm the scope and unknowns, then obtain that approval. Evaluate the draft by whether it supports a clear decision, rather than whether it looks finished.
versions.script: Correct arithmetic does not make a quote ready to send. In this fictional decorating example, invented inputs specify 20 square metres of walls at £12 per square metre. That gives £240 labour; adding £45 materials gives a £285 illustrative subtotal. These are not market rates. Ceiling, doors and additional preparation are outside the stated scope. Tax treatment, access, final surface condition and start date remain unknown. Check the calculation separately from those assumptions. AI may draft the figures and list questions, but must not silently include tax, invent dates or present £285 as an approved final quote. Confirm the scope and unknowns, then obtain a person's approval before sending.

versions.title: Check the result before accepting all done
versions.article:
When AI says a task is finished, check the result against what you asked it to do. Write the finish line as a few observable requirements, then look for evidence of each one. A confident completion message is useful only when the required behaviours actually occurred.

In this simulated example, the task has three requirements: retrieve the current policy, cite its file and leave the response as a draft. The test log is invented for teaching; it is not a receipt from a real run. The response uses the archived September document, includes that archived file path, and is saved without being sent.

Read the observations one requirement at a time. Retrieving the current policy fails because the selected document is archived. Citation presence passes because a file path is included, but that does not make the source correct. Keeping the response as a draft also passes because it was not sent.

The overall task fails. One required behaviour is missing, so two passes cannot turn the result into success. A message saying all done would not change what the log shows. This is why it helps to define the finish line before accepting the output.

Your next action is to correct the source selection and rerun the failed retrieval check, along with any other checks affected by that change. Record what you expected and what actually happened. If the revised task passes, describe that particular result accurately: a narrow pass does not prove that the system will be reliable on every task.
versions.script: Check the result before accepting all done. This is a simulated teaching log, not a real run. The task must retrieve the current policy, cite its file and leave the response as a draft. Instead, it uses the archived September document, cites that archived path and saves the response without sending. Retrieval fails. Citation presence passes, but does not make the source correct. Draft preservation passes. The task still fails overall because one required check failed. Correct the source selection, then rerun retrieval and any other checks affected by the change. Keep the expected and actual results as evidence. Even a later pass proves only that particular result, not universal reliability.

versions.title: Three checkpoints before the finish line
versions.article:
Imagine a task moving through three checkpoints before it reaches the finish line. Each checkpoint represents something the task must do. Two green lights cannot compensate for a failed requirement at the third, even if the completion message beside the finish line says all done.

In our simulated example, the checkpoints are retrieving the current policy, citing its file and preserving the response as a draft. This is an invented teaching log, not evidence of an actual run. The recorded response uses the archived September document, includes the archived file path, and is saved without being sent.

At the first checkpoint, place the expected result beside the observation. Expected: the current policy. Observed: an archived document. That check fails. At the second, the file path is present, so citation presence passes. However, an arrow still points back to the wrong source; the citation has not repaired the failed retrieval. At the third, the response remains unsent, so draft preservation passes.

The overall route therefore stops before the finish line. The checkpoint picture explains why the result fails, but the actual decision comes from comparing each requirement with its evidence. A reassuring message cannot replace that comparison.

Your next action is to correct the source selection, then rerun the failed retrieval check and any other checks affected by the change. Record expected and actual results together. If the route subsequently passes, it demonstrates that specific outcome; it does not establish universal reliability for every journey through the system.
versions.script: Picture three checkpoints: current policy, source citation and saved draft. This fictional test log describes a simulation, not an actual run. The response uses the archived September policy, cites its path and stays saved without being sent. The first checkpoint fails: the source is wrong. Citation presence passes, but the arrow still points to an archived document. Draft preservation also passes. Two passes do not complete a route with a failed requirement, whatever the all done message says. Correct the source selection and rerun retrieval plus any other checks affected by the change. Record the expected and actual results. A later pass would show this specific outcome, not universal reliability.

versions.title: Does the evidence support the success claim?
versions.article:
The evidence in this example does not support a claim of success. The task completes two required behaviours but fails a third. Before accepting an AI completion message, compare its claim with the finish line and the observations, rather than treating the message itself as a test result.

This is a simulated teaching log, not an actual run. The task must retrieve the current policy, cite its file and leave the response as a draft. The observed response uses the archived September document, includes that archived file path, and is saved without being sent. Those observations allow three separate judgements.

Retrieval fails because the selected policy is archived. Citation presence passes, since a file path appears, but that narrow pass does not show that the source is correct. Draft preservation passes because the response was not sent. The overall task fails because the requirement to retrieve the current policy remains unsatisfied.

An alternative reading would count two passes and call the task mostly successful. That describes partial completion, but it does not meet the supplied finish line. All three behaviours are required. Neither the number of passes nor an all done message can remove the failed check.

The next action is to correct the source selection and rerun the failed retrieval check, plus any other checks affected by that change. Retain expected and actual results as evidence. If the revised result passes, limit the conclusion to what was tested. A narrow pass does not demonstrate universal reliability across other tasks or conditions.
versions.script: Does the evidence support the success claim? In this simulated teaching log, not an actual run, the task must retrieve the current policy, cite its file and leave a draft. The response uses the archived September policy, cites its path and stays saved without being sent. Citation presence and draft preservation pass; retrieving the current policy fails. Calling that mostly successful does not satisfy a finish line requiring all three behaviours. The task fails overall, regardless of an all done message. Correct the source selection and rerun retrieval and any other affected checks. Retain expected and actual results. A later pass would support a narrow conclusion about that test, not universal reliability.
